newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's telecoms win tariff campaign.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's telecoms win tariff campaign.

text.p: Argentina's Telecom and Telefonica have won a long fight to overhaul telephone tariffs and are well-placed to compete in an open market after 2000, analysts say.

Stockbrokers expected their shares and ADRS to add to the gains from recent earnings news and analysts hailed the end of a campaign that became bogged down in politics as soon as the state telephone monopoly ENTEL was privatized in 1990.
"Basically the companies have been given what they wanted," William Beavington, Paribas Capital Markets' telecoms analyst in Wall Street told Reuters by telephone.

But the angry reaction from consumer groups and opposition parties, who all argued in public hearings on tariffs ending in December 1996 that private users' telephone bills would rise and phone companies would pocket the difference, came quickly.
"These increases show tremendous injustice," Ombudsman Jorge Maiorano said.
He was awaiting the presidential decree in the Official Bulletin to confirm the rate changes, but said: "I absolutely do not rule out starting an appeal."

Telecom and Telefonica had long been lobbying for cuts in long-distance and international call rates, which they said would make charges fairer for business and help them become more competitive by the time the Argentine phone market is thrown open to all competitors, probably in the year 2000.
Under the privatization agreement, they were given seven years' exclusivity which ends this year, with three more years of virtual duopoly if they meet certain agreed targets.

"There is definitely short-term upside in their shares here because it removes the cloud of uncertainty. We can now see that by 2000 these companies should be in a stronger position to compete internationally," said Beavington.

Details of the tariff changes released by Telecom show the rates for the longest distance domestic calls fall 56 percent and international calls by an average of 42 percent. But urban call rates rise, there are no more free pulses and monthly rental charges are hiked up.

The firms had lobbied for residential rental of $16.1 a month, commercial rent of $31 and "professional" rent of $22.2 a month. In fact, residential rent rose to $12.49, commercial rates to $32 and professional rental to $24.40.

"What they lose straight away on international charges coming down, they gain immediately on monthly charges going up," said one local telecoms analyst. "It looks like a very good tariff rebalancing for the telephone companies. But let's keep a look-out for the reactions."
He did not have to wait for long.

"The telephone companies have won," protested Ombudsman Maiorano, while members of Congress of the opposition Radical Party and Frepaso started up public campaigns in protest and Jorge Casabe of consumer group ADECUA said his group would take legal action to defend consumers.

With papers like Clarin carrying the front-page headline "Sharp Rises in Phone Rates Decreed" and emphasizing strong profits made by Telecom and Telefonica since privatization, the government tried a counter-offensive.
Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez told reporters the increase in the general public's phone bills would be "insignificant" and the tariff changes were not exactly what the firms wanted.
He also argued the new monthly rent was "comparatively at the same level or lower than in most countries in the world."

Telecom stressed there was "no way the rebalancing could mean higher earnings for the companies" and said in its own case, if tariff revenue exceeded $134 million a year it would have to plough that back into call rate reductions.
"The bottom line has always been that the government was going to make certain the rebalanced tariffs were going to be revenue neutral," said Paribas' Beavington.
